# Cup Day: 140 Covers, One Dead Coolroom and 30kg of Laneway Beef

Right, Jonno. You’ve sent approximately forty messages asking what happened with the coolroom on Cup Day, so here it is. The full story. I’m not typing it into WhatsApp in bits between you asking follow-up questions from London like you’re filing a report for the BBC.

You’d have lost your mind if you were here. Properly lost it. London’s made you soft, but even old, pre-London Jonno would’ve stood in front of that coolroom reading the thermometer over and over like it might apologise.

So, for everyone else: the compressor died sometime between Monday night and Tuesday morning. Cup Day morning. Tuesday 3 November. Naturally.

I found it at 6.40am. Thermometer said 11 degrees.

Eleven.

Not ideal for a coolroom, unless we’d decided to pivot into being a slightly chilly storage cupboard. We had 140 covers booked for lunch, all on the three-course set menu, and the thing keeping most of that lunch cold had quietly carked it overnight.

Raff was away, so it was me running the show. Phil’s contribution was the classic management masterstroke: “Just make it work, mate.”

Thanks, Phil. Why didn’t I think of that? Here I was about to try the opposite approach.

That is not a plan, by the way. “Just make it work” is what you say when you don’t want to look at a problem but would still like to take partial credit if somebody else fixes it.

I called Wally from Coldline. Wally could not come until Wednesday because the part was coming from Sydney, which is excellent news when you’re standing in Melbourne on Tuesday morning with a coolroom doing a very convincing impression of autumn.

So we started moving everything.

The two undercounters got packed first. Then the bar fridge, which immediately stopped being a bar fridge and became a highly inefficient meat and dairy cabinet. After that it was a matter of opening doors, staring into spaces that were already full, and trying to make more space through aggression.

That’s when Marta from the café next door gave us half her walk-in.

Marta saved Cup Day. Important that we acknowledge that before we get to the part where she financially enslaved me in pastries.

She didn’t want cash. She wanted croissant credit. I now owe her roughly three weeks of staff meals’ worth, and honestly, I think she’s coming out ahead. She saw an opportunity and took it. Respect.

This is how Benny and I ended up moving 30kg of beef shin down the laneway on a milk crate trolley.

In the rain.

Because of course it was raining.

There’s a special kind of focus that comes over you when you’re wheeling an entire lunch service down a wet laneway at breakfast time. No music, no conversation, just the little trolley wheels rattling and both of us silently begging the beef not to become somebody else’s problem on the footpath.

Then one wheel fell off.

Not wobbled. Not made a funny noise. Fell off.

Jonno, you’d have cried there. I’m confident about that. You’d have sat down next to the milk crate and started asking why these things always happen to us, while Benny and I picked up 30kg of wet beef shin and pretended you were still useful back in London.

Somehow we got it all into Marta’s walk-in. The rest of the stock was spread between the undercounters, the bar fridge and Kev’s emergency esky operation.

Kev, our dishy, went to the servo and came back with fourteen bags of ice. Fourteen. The bloke behind the counter asked if we were having a party.

Yes, mate. A very exclusive party where everyone’s stressed and the dairy’s going off.

We still lost about $1,800 worth of stock, mostly dairy and the duck legs. Not ideal. But at that point we’d stopped treating the morning as a disaster and started treating it as a weirdly expensive obstacle course.

The impressive part was that lunch still looked like lunch from the other side of the pass. Tickets came in, food went out, and nobody dining had any idea that half the kitchen was being refrigerated by a bar fridge and the other half was down a laneway under Marta’s increasingly expensive supervision.

Well. Almost nobody.

At 12.15 we had to 86 the panna cotta. There was no saving it, and serving it would’ve turned the dessert course into something considerably more memorable than anyone wanted.

So dessert became “affogato with whatever”.

That was not the official menu description, although in hindsight we should’ve printed it. People loved it. Possibly more than they love the panna cotta, which is rude but fair. There’s something about nearly losing an entire kitchen that really frees you up creatively. Can’t serve the planned dessert? Fine. Coffee, ice cream, whatever’s still cold, off you go.

We might make it a permanent thing. “Affogato with Whatever” sounds like something a restaurant with exposed brick would charge $24 for.

Then the lady on table 9 asked whether the beef was “free range from the laneway” because she’d seen Benny and me out the window earlier with the trolley.

Fair enough. Good question. Honestly, for a few minutes there, the beef had more freedom of movement than any of us.

She thought she was very funny. Unfortunately, she was.

The whole service had this strange energy where everyone just locked in. No standing around, no debating whose job something was, no disappearing for ten minutes when a section got busy. Everyone knew the coolroom was dead, the stock was scattered across half the postcode and Phil’s grand strategy was “mate”.

So we just got on with it.

Kev kept the esky stocked. Benny kept moving. Marta kept her side of the walk-in open and her croissant ledger updated. I spent most of the day opening one fridge to get something, finding three things that belonged in another fridge, then forgetting why I’d opened the first fridge.

And somehow, it was the best service we did all year.

I hate saying that because it sounds like I’m agreeing with Phil. I’m not. If you’re reading this, Phil, we are not replacing the Preventative Maintenance Plan with “the staff will probably cope”.

Good service is not a refrigeration strategy.

But yeah, everyone was brilliant. Not in a big inspirational-speech way. Nobody stood on a milk crate and talked about believing in each other. The milk crates were structurally unsound anyway. It was just a full kitchen of people doing exactly what needed doing, at speed, while everything around us got steadily more ridiculous.

Meanwhile, my horse in the Cup sweep was called Ice Cold Lad.

You can’t make that up.

After the morning I’d had, I thought perhaps the universe was finally throwing me something. Ice Cold Lad. Coolroom disaster. Bit of nominative destiny. Perhaps he’d come storming home, I’d win the sweep and recover at least part of the duck-leg money.

He came second last.

Second. Last.

So no, the universe wasn’t offering compensation. It was taking the piss.

By the end of the day I’d run 140 covers through a three-course lunch, lost a coolroom, lost $1,800 of stock, lost a trolley wheel, gained an unspecified croissant debt and finished with a dessert I’d made up while lunch was already happening. The only reliable thing left was Kev’s esky and my growing suspicion that bar fridges are built tougher than coolrooms.

That’s the big lesson, Jonno. Bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite.

Also Marta. Mostly Marta, on Cup Day.

Anyway, that’s what happened. You can stop messaging me now. Go enjoy London, where I assume coolrooms politely email you three weeks before breaking down and someone named Oliver arrives with a contingency plan.

You’d have been completely useless here. I wish you’d been there.

Come home, ya flog. There’s still a spot for you on grill, and I know a lady next door who accepts croissants.
